analysis.one_liner: Bans drug companies from paying generic or biosimilar rivals to keep cheaper versions off the market.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee in a 28-13 vote in September 2021, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a brand-name drug company is sued by a generic maker over a patent, the two sometimes settle with the brand company paying the generic company to stay off the market for a while — a "pay-for-delay" deal that keeps cheaper copies from reaching pharmacies. This bill would make those deals unlawful. The Federal Trade Commission could go after the companies, with penalties up to three times what they gained, and a generic maker that took such a deal would lose its valuable 180-day head start as the first approved generic. Legitimate settlements were still allowed. The bill cleared the House Judiciary Committee 28-13 but never got a vote by the full House, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone who fills a prescription. Pay-for-delay deals can delay cheaper generic versions of drugs by months or years, during which people pay brand-name prices. By presuming such deals unlawful and letting the FTC act, the bill would have sped up generic and biosimilar competition, which typically drives prices down sharply once multiple copies reach the market. Taxpayers benefit too, since Medicare and Medicaid absorb much of the cost of delayed competition.

how_it_helps.text: It treats as unlawful any patent settlement in which the generic or biosimilar maker receives something of value and agrees to stay off the market for a period of time.

It lets the FTC enforce the ban, with penalties up to three times the value the companies gained from the delay, and it requires companies to certify that they have disclosed the complete agreement to the FTC and Justice Department, including oral side deals [S3].
A generic maker that violates it loses the valuable 180-day exclusivity period that normally rewards the first generic challenger [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies, which would lose the ability to pay generic makers to delay competition, and generic makers that profit from those deals. Consumers and insurers would pay less.

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a presumption that any settlement involving payment and delay is anticompetitive, and the companies bear the burden of proving otherwise by clear and convincing evidence — a heavy standard that could penalize settlements that are actually pro-competitive, since the bill explicitly forbids the fact-finder from assuming that a pre-expiry entry date shows a deal was beneficial [S3].

The threat of penalties up to triple the value received could make brand-name and generic manufacturers more reluctant to settle patent disputes at all, meaning more drawn-out litigation — and in some cases a settlement that lets a generic reach the market early might be replaced by years in court with the generic fully blocked [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and broadly distributed: pay-for-delay settlements are a well-documented practice where a brand-name maker pays a generic maker to stay off the market, and the FTC has estimated these deals cost consumers billions of dollars a year in the form of higher drug prices. The main cost falls on pharmaceutical companies, whose settlement freedom would be curtailed. The strongest good-faith objections are that the presumption is one-sided — a settlement that simply lets the generic sell earlier could still be challenged unless the parties prove otherwise — and that a burden this heavy might discourage companies from settling patent disputes at all, leading to more litigation and possibly delaying some generic launches that settlements would have accelerated. On balance the bill targeted a specific practice that raises drug prices, and its carve-outs for ordinary early-entry settlements address the most common objection.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee voted 28-13 to advance the bill on September 29, 2021, but it was never taken up by the full House, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 28, 2021 by Rep. Jerrold Nadler with bipartisan cosponsors, including three Republicans [S1].
It was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, then to the Health Subcommittee [S5].
On September 29, 2021, the Judiciary Committee voted 28-13 to order the bill reported with a substitute, a sign of committee-level support [S5].
No further action was recorded; the bill was never reported to the full House or given a floor vote, and it died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023 [S1, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies that use settlement payments to delay generic competition kept that tool available, and consumers kept paying brand-name prices where those deals occur.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers that paid to delay generics

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, oversaw its markup.

for.name: 28 of 42 House Judiciary Committee members voting
for.what_they_did: Voted 28-13 to order the bill reported to the House with a substitute.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry has historically opposed pay-for-delay legislation, arguing settlements are legitimate patent litigation resolutions; no industry opposition appears in the provided record.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 4 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored — and the committee vote of 28-13 shows support across the committee, though the record does not break the roll call down by party.

industries.note: The bill makes it unlawful and costly to pay generic or biosimilar rivals to delay market entry, ending one way brand companies extend monopoly pricing after patents begin to lapse. Their interest runs against patients, who pay higher prices during the delayed period.

Generic makers can no longer accept payment for staying out of the market, closing off a lucrative deal type, but they gain the right to challenge such deals and compete earlier. First-filing generic makers lose the 180-day exclusivity if they violate the law.
Not a named target of the bill, but indirectly affected: delayed generic entry keeps drug costs and premiums higher, so faster generic competition would ease their costs as well as patients'.
